response.internal_assessment: I gave myself the two weeks. I did the reading. I know what the app looks like, I know the fare structure, I know there is a 15-minute wait and that it will improve. I know that two people in Millfield have already moved away from their cars this month — James Patterson is one of them, and James is not careless. What I found at the library was not frightening. The app is simpler than the telehealth portal I helped Edna Marsh navigate last Tuesday, and Edna is 79 with arthritic fingers. I can do this. The question I am sitting with now is not whether I can learn the technology. The question is whether I am willing to let what I learn from actually using it change my thinking — and that is a harder question, because it involves the car, and the car involves things I have not said out loud to anyone. I think the honest answer is: yes. I am willing. But I want one low-stakes test before I decide anything about the $281.

chosen_actions.description: Download the RoboRide app on my phone this week — the library aide Marcus can help me if I get stuck — and book one short test ride. The destination will be the Millfield Community Center on Thursday afternoon, which I was already planning to walk to for the drop-in hours Lisa expanded. It is 1.4 miles. At $0.18/mile that is roughly 25 cents plus whatever base fare applies. I am not evaluating whether to give up the car. I am evaluating whether the app works, whether the vehicle is clean and safe, whether the wait is what they say it is, and whether I feel dignified at the end of it.
chosen_actions.resources_involved: Time plus approximately $3-5 for fare. No financial commitment to anything larger.
chosen_actions.reasoning: There is a difference between understanding a thing and having done it. I taught that for 37 years. I read everything I could find about RoboRide at the library and I learned nothing that told me what it actually feels like to sit in one of those vehicles and arrive somewhere. I need that data point. I am choosing the Community Center because it is familiar, because I was going anyway, and because if something goes wrong I am four blocks from Patricia's office and I can call her. The stakes are low enough that a bad experience will be informative rather than frightening, and a good experience will be genuinely meaningful.

chosen_actions.description: Attend Maria Santos' public input session on the RoboRide rollout. Not as someone who has decided anything, but as someone who has done some homework and has questions worth contributing. I will listen for what the auto row workers are feeling. I heard through the book group that Betty's diner is worried about lunch traffic. Carlos Ruiz apparently has his eye on EV certification courses. These are real people navigating real things and the council should hear from the full picture, not just the loudest voices. If I am asked to speak I will say: I am a 72-year-old retired teacher who just booked her first robotaxi ride this week, and here is what I found.
chosen_actions.reasoning: Maria's statement was plain-spoken and honest. She said 'you will not be left to face this alone' and I believe she meant it. I have been part of this community for 31 years. I have opinions about what good transition policy looks like — I watched my school district navigate three rounds of curriculum upheaval and I know the difference between a process that pretends to consult and one that actually listens. My voice at that meeting is worth something, and I owe it to Betty and Carlos and the others to show up.

chosen_actions.description: After the test ride and before the town hall, sit down at the kitchen table and write out, privately, two columns: what the car actually costs me per month in real numbers, and what I actually use it for. Not what I used to use it for. Not what I might need it for in a theoretical emergency. What I have actually driven to, and how often, over the past three months. I have the gas receipts and the mileage log I keep for the insurance. I will do the arithmetic honestly.
chosen_actions.reasoning: I am a person who makes decisions with information. The $281 monthly payment is real money — it is a choice I am making every month, and I have not looked at it clearly in two years because looking at it clearly would require me to ask whether it is still the right choice. I am not ready to answer that question yet. But I am ready to look at it. Those are different things and it matters that I know the difference.

response.emotional_state: Quieter than last tick. The unsettled feeling has not gone away but it has stopped being uncomfortable — it has become the texture of paying attention, which I recognize. The curiosity is no longer tentative. I am not performing openness. I am open.
response.inner_monologue: If it goes badly I will have a story to tell at the book group, and if it goes well I am going to have to have a conversation with myself that I have been postponing for two years.
